section.heading: 11.4. Series with Positive Terms
section.paragraph: The convergence or divergence of a telescoping series or a geometric series is relatively easy to determine because we can find a simple formula for the $$N$$ th partial sum $$S_{N}$$ of these series. Very often, obtaining a simple formula for the $$N$$ th partial sum of an infinite series is difficult or impossible, and we are forced to look for alternative ways to investigate the convergence or divergence of the series.

In this section, we look at several tests for determining the convergence or divergence of an infinite series by examining its $$n$$ th term $$a_{n}$$ . These tests will confirm the convergence of a series without yielding a value for its sum. Often, this is all that is needed. Once it has been ascertained that a series is convergent, we can approximate its sum to any degree of accuracy desired by adding up the terms of its $$N$$ th partial sum $$S_{N}$$ , provided that $$N$$ is chosen large enough.
Our first test tells us how to identify a divergent series.
section.heading: The Test for Divergence
section.paragraph: The following theorem tells us that the terms of a convergent series must ultimately approach zero.

An important consequence of Theorem 3 is the following useful test for divergence.

note.title: Theorem 4. The Test for Divergence
note.heading: Theorem 4. The Test for Divergence
note.paragraph: If $$\lim\limits_{n\rightarrow\infty}a_{n}$$ does not exist or $$\lim\limits_{n\rightarrow\infty}a_{n} \neq 0$$ , then $$\sum\limits_{n = 1}^{\infty}a_{n}$$ diverges.

section.paragraph: Observe that the test for divergence does not say that if $$\lim\limits_{n\rightarrow\infty}a_{n} = 0$$ , then $$\sum\limits_{n = 1}^{\infty}a_{n}$$ must converge. In other words, the converse of Theorem 4 is not true in general. For example, $$\lim\limits_{n\rightarrow\infty}\frac{1}{n} = 0$$ , yet, as we will see later, the harmonic series $$\sum\limits_{n = 1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{n}$$ is divergent. (See Example 3.) In short, the test for divergence rules out convergence for a series whose $$n$$ th term does not approach zero but yields no information if the $$n$$ th term of a series does approach zero; that is, the series may or may not converge.

section.paragraph: We now look at several tests that tell us whether a series is convergent. These tests apply only to series with positive terms.
section.heading: The Integral Test
section.paragraph: The integral test ties the convergence or divergence of an infinite series $$\sum\limits_{n = 1}^{\infty}a_{n}$$ to the convergence or divergence of the improper integral $$\int_{1}^{\infty}{f(x)\mathit{dx}}$$ , where $$f(n) = a_{n}$$ .

list.item: The integral test simply tells us whether a series converges or diverges. If it indicates that a series converges, we may not conclude that the (finite) value of the improper integral used in conjunction with the test is the sum of the convergent series.

Since the convergence of an infinite series is not affected by the omission or addition of a finite number of terms to the series, we sometimes study the series $${\sum\limits_{n = N}^{\infty}a_{n}} = a_{N} + a_{N + 1} + \cdots$$ rather than the series $$\sum\limits_{n = 1}^{\infty}a_{n}$$ . In this case, the series is compared to the improper integral $$\int_{N}^{\infty}{f{(x)}\mathit{dx}}$$ as we will see in Example 4.

note.paragraph: A $$p$$ -series is a series of the form

section.paragraph: Observe that for $$p = 1$$ , the $$p$$ -series is just the harmonic series $$\sum\limits_{n = 1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{n}$$ . The conditions for the convergence or divergence of the $$p$$ -series can be found by applying the integral test to the series.

note.title: Theorem 6. Convergence of p -Series
note.heading: Theorem 6. Convergence of p -Series
note.paragraph: The $$p$$ -series $$\sum\limits_{n = 1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{n^{p}}$$ converges if $$p > 1$$ and diverges if $$p \leq 1$$ .

section.paragraph: Proof If $$p < 0$$ , then
$$\lim\limits_{n\rightarrow\infty}\frac{1}{n^{p}} = \infty$$
If $$p = 0$$ , then
$$\lim\limits_{n\rightarrow\infty}\frac{1}{n^{p}} = 1$$

In either case, $$\lim\limits_{n\rightarrow\infty}\frac{1}{n^{p}} \neq 0$$ so the $$p$$ -series diverges by the test for divergence. If $$p > 0$$ , then the function $$f{(x)} = 1 \slash x^{p}$$ is continuous, positive, and decreasing on $$\left\lbrack 1,\infty) \right.$$ . It can be shown that $$\int_{1}^{\infty}{\frac{1}{x^{p}}\mathit{dx}}$$ converges if $$p > 1$$ and diverges if $$p \leq 1$$ (see Exercise 53). Using this result and the integral test, we conclude that $$\sum\limits_{n = 1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{n^{p}}$$ converges if $$p > 1$$ and diverges if $$0 < p \leq 1$$ . Therefore, $$\sum\limits_{n = 1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{n^{p}}$$ converges if $$p > 1$$ and diverges if $$p \leq 1$$ .

section.heading: The Comparison Test
section.paragraph: The convergence or divergence of a given series $$\text{Σ} a_{n}$$ can sometimes be determined by comparing its terms with the terms of a test series that is known to be convergent or divergent. This is the basis for the comparison test for series that follows. In the rest of this section, we assume that all series under consideration have positive terms.

Suppose that the terms of a series $$\text{Σ} a_{n}$$ are smaller than the corresponding terms of a series $$\text{Σ} b_{n}$$ . This situation is illustrated in Figure 7, where the respective terms are represented by rectangles, each of width $$1$$ and appropriate height.

figure.caption: Each rectangle representing $$a_{n}$$ is contained in the rectangle representing $$b_{n}$$ .

section.paragraph: If $$\text{Σ} b_{n}$$ is convergent, the total area of the rectangles representing this series is finite. Since each rectangle representing the terms of the series $$\text{Σ} a_{n}$$ is contained in a corresponding rectangle representing the terms of $$\text{Σ} b_{n}$$ , the total area of the rectangles representing $$\text{Σ} a_{n}$$ must also be finite; that is, the series $$\text{Σ} a_{n}$$ must be convergent. A similar argument would seem to suggest that if all the terms of a series $$\text{Σ} a_{n}$$ are larger than the corresponding terms of a series $$\text{Σ} b_{n}$$ that is known to be divergent, then $$\text{Σ} a_{n}$$ must itself be divergent. These observations lead to the following theorem.

note.title: Theorem 7. The Comparison Test
note.heading: Theorem 7. The Comparison Test
note.paragraph: Suppose that $$\text{Σ} a_{n}$$ and $$\text{Σ} b_{n}$$ are series with positive terms.

list.item: If $$\text{Σ} b_{n}$$ is convergent and $$a_{n} \leq b_{n}$$ for all $$n$$ , then $$\text{Σ} a_{n}$$ is also convergent.
If $$\text{Σ} b_{n}$$ is divergent and $$a_{n} \geq b_{n}$$ for all $$n$$ , then $$\text{Σ} a_{n}$$ is also divergent.

section.paragraph: Here is an intuitive justification for Theorem 7. Let
and

be the $$N$$ th terms of the sequence of partial sums of $$\text{Σ} a_{n}$$ and $$\text{Σ} b_{n}$$ , respectively. Since both series have positive terms, $$\left\{ S_{N} \right\}$$ and $$\left\{ T_{N} \right\}$$ are increasing.

list.item: If $$\sum\limits_{n = 1}^{\infty}b_{n}$$ is convergent, then there exists a number $$L$$ such that $$\lim\limits_{N\rightarrow\infty}T_{N} = L$$ and $$T_{N} \leq L$$ for all $$N$$ . Since $$a_{n} \leq b_{n}$$ for all $$n$$ , we have $$S_{N} \leq T_{N}$$ , and this implies that $$S_{N} \leq L$$ for all $$N$$ . We have shown that $$\left\{ S_{N} \right\}$$ is increasing and bounded above, so, as before, we can argue intuitively that $$S_{N}$$ and therefore $$\text{Σ} a_{n}$$ converges.

If $$\text{Σ} b_{n}$$ is divergent, then $$\lim\limits_{N\rightarrow\infty}T_{N} = \infty$$ , since $$\left\{ T_{N} \right\}$$ is increasing. But $$a_{n} \geq b_{n}$$ for all $$n$$ , and this implies that $$S_{N} \geq T_{N}$$ , which in turn implies that $$\lim\limits_{N\rightarrow\infty}S_{N} = \infty$$ . Therefore, $$\text{Σ} a_{n}$$ diverges.

note.title: Notes
note.heading: Notes
note.paragraph: Since the convergence or divergence of a series is not affected by the omission of a finite number of terms of the series, the condition $$a_{n} \leq b_{n}$$ (or $$a_{n} \geq b_{n}$$ ) for all $$n$$ can be replaced by the condition that these inequalities hold for all $$n \geq k$$ for some integer $$k$$ .

section.paragraph: To use Theorem 7, we need a catalog of test series whose convergence and divergence are known. In what follows, we will use the geometric series and the $$p$$ -series as test series.
